1. New investment in sunset technology 

Does this grow a system that sits outside our agreed future ('target') set-up, instead of moving us toward it?

2. Investment off the target architecture

Does this grow a system that sits outside our agreed future ('target') set-up, instead of moving us toward it?

3. Duplicate of an enterprise capability

Are we paying for something a shared, company-wide system already does?

4. No or weak business case

Is the spend hard to justify — no clear benefits, no owner, or it won't pay back in time?

5. Low strategic fit

Can we actually connect this to a stated company or business priority?

6. Incremental fragmentation

Is this yet another small one-off add-on, rather than part of a planned, bundled improvement?

7. Paying for unused capacity

Are we buying more licences or capacity while a lot of what we already own sits unused?

8. Deepens lock-in / raises exit cost

Does this make us more dependent on a supplier we plan to leave — harder or costlier to exit later?

9. Fully deferrable

Could we simply postpone this for a year or more with no real harm?

Named authority & instrument

Can we point to the actual law, regulation, or tax rule that requires this — chapter and verse?

Mandatory, not discretionary

Does the rule genuinely force this, or is it really our own choice or best practice?

Applicability confirmed (Legal / Compliance / Tax)

Has someone qualified (Legal / Compliance / Tax) confirmed the rule really applies to this specific part of Philips?

Independent second-line validation

Has an independent team — not the sponsor — formally signed this off?

Minimum-viable scope

Are we doing only what the rule requires, or adding 'nice-to-have' extras on top?

Impact — how serious the consequence is if we don't comply

If we don't comply, how serious is the consequence?

Likelihood — how likely it is to happen if we don't act

How likely is it to actually happen if we don't act?

Deadline — how close the mandatory date is

How soon is the date by which we must comply?

TMS market implementations : A central solution is needed to unlock the potential for Markets to fully utilize TMID. Until now, the industrial  / upstream side has been focus. to implement this for International Markets

Parcel solution implementation - Our current parcel solutions (Clippership, Process Weaver, current TMID OE solution) are scattered and not in line with Philips policy. TMID does not cater for a high volume labeling creation solution at this moment, nor does it have a proper link to the US customs for AES filing. This means: No visibility, no PoD management, limited T&T, no support – and ad hoc tribal knowledge. A new solution would allow to seamlessly integrate any request from our business and to void non-policy solutions. Automated AES filing is not done anymore by suppliers but Philips; AES validates data in real time and flags errors immediately, allowing corrections before export rather than discovering issues after shipment or during an audit. This reduces misclassification, incorrect values, or license errors (no costs for external parties if used).

This initiative will reserve and secure dedicated operations funding, enable an EI-owned Microsoft Project Operations support team, avoid service continuity risk, reduce manual workarounds and improve cost transparency and data quality.

PD has significant cost competitiveness opportunities across material cost, logistics, service, installation, quality and third-party spend, but these opportunities are fragmented across businesses and functions and are not consistently converted into measurable, Finance-validated savings. Limited cost transparency, inconsistent baselines, late identification of performance gaps and overlapping improvement activities make it difficult to distinguish incremental opportunities from existing AOP commitments, prioritize the highest-value interventions and demonstrate sustainable benefit realization.

Examples illustrate the issue: quotation decisions can rely on material costs that are no longer current; €2.3M–€5.3M of logistics opportunity has already been identified but requires validation to convert into committed savings; and in 2026, €18.8M of the logistics gap remained unclosed, demonstrating the value of earlier visibility and intervention. In parallel, opportunities in e-component procurement, remote service, FSE capacity and installation cost are largely execution-led and sit within BU cost bases, creating a need to avoid duplication and clearly separate enabling investment from BU-owned execution.

A coordinated PD-wide cost competitiveness approach is therefore needed to provide earlier and more reliable cost transparency, establish consistent baselines and benefit attribution, consolidate overlapping opportunities, and enable BUs to convert identified opportunities into sustainable, auditable savings while retaining ownership of the underlying P&L benefits.

Establish a cross-PD cost competitiveness program to identify, validate, execute, and track structural cost reduction, cost avoidance, and productivity opportunities across material and procurement, logistics, service, installation and cost-to-serve, quality, packaging, third-party spend, training, IFU creation, and AI-enabled productivity, using connected data, standardized cross-BU approaches, reusable automation, and ProductivityOne for activity tracking and Finance-validated value realization.

1. Non-Entitleable Strategic Parts: Automates strategic parts entitlement, reducing manual effort, improving service accuracy, and protecting service revenue.
2. Selective Part Return:  Reduces unnecessary part returns, lowering logistics costs and improving investigation efficiency.
3. FCO vs Service Parts Stock Segregation: Separates FCO and service stock to improve inventory control, FCO execution, compliance, and traceability.

1. Non-entitleable strategic parts : Philips will continue relying on manual CEN creation and customer claims processes, resulting in service delays, missed or incorrect entitlements, reduced visibility for FSEs and customers, and ongoing revenue leakage from lost upsell opportunities and inaccurate entitlement execution
2. Selective part return:Philips will continue incurring avoidable reverse logistics, handling, and investigation costs by returning non-relevant parts, while quality teams experience slower investigations and reduced focus on critical failures.
3. FCO Vs service part segregation: Without this, FCO campaigns will continue to face parts shortages, delayed field implementation, weak installed-base traceability, higher manual effort, and increased compliance and customer-service risk.

1.  Several strategic service parts cannot be managed as true entitlements in ServiceMax and therefore require manual Customer Experience Notes to track coverage. This creates manual effort, entitlement visibility gaps, service delays, customer claims processing, and potential revenue leakage throughout the contract lifecycle.
2. Current return process forces all parts matching a logistics group to be returned, regardless of whether they are relevant for quality investigation. This results in unnecessary logistics, handling and investigation costs.
3. FCO and routine service parts share the same inventory, causing manual workarounds, poor traceability, compliance risk, and delays in executing field upgrades.

1. Non-entiteable strategic parts - Enable strategic parts to be managed as standard ServiceMax entitlements by introducing new material classifications, maintaining part-to-classification mappings, and making entitlements visible and reportable across SAP and ServiceMax. This covers contract quoting, booking, entitlement checks, parts fulfillment, and customer portal visibility.
2. Selective part return - Introduce a selective return capability in ServiceMax/SAP that allows parts to be returned based on predefined criteria such as entitlement type, failure classification, part category, or criticality. The scope covers FRU return management, reverse logistics, parts handling, and investigation processes
3. FCO vs service parts stock segregation - Implement inventory segregation between FCO and service parts while maintaining proper Installed Base updates and service workflows. The solution will support inventory planning, allocation, tracking, and execution of FCO activities across businesses using SAP and ServiceMax processes.

1. New investment in sunset technology 

Does this grow a system that sits outside our agreed future ('target') set-up, instead of moving us toward it?

2. Investment off the target architecture

Does this grow a system that sits outside our agreed future ('target') set-up, instead of moving us toward it?

3. Duplicate of an enterprise capability

Are we paying for something a shared, company-wide system already does?

4. No or weak business case

Is the spend hard to justify — no clear benefits, no owner, or it won't pay back in time?

5. Low strategic fit

Can we actually connect this to a stated company or business priority?

6. Incremental fragmentation

Is this yet another small one-off add-on, rather than part of a planned, bundled improvement?

7. Paying for unused capacity

Are we buying more licences or capacity while a lot of what we already own sits unused?

8. Deepens lock-in / raises exit cost

Does this make us more dependent on a supplier we plan to leave — harder or costlier to exit later?

9. Fully deferrable

Could we simply postpone this for a year or more with no real harm?

Named authority & instrument

Can we point to the actual law, regulation, or tax rule that requires this — chapter and verse?

Mandatory, not discretionary

Does the rule genuinely force this, or is it really our own choice or best practice?

Applicability confirmed (Legal / Compliance / Tax)

Has someone qualified (Legal / Compliance / Tax) confirmed the rule really applies to this specific part of Philips?

Independent second-line validation

Has an independent team — not the sponsor — formally signed this off?

Minimum-viable scope

Are we doing only what the rule requires, or adding 'nice-to-have' extras on top?

Impact — how serious the consequence is if we don't comply

If we don't comply, how serious is the consequence?

Likelihood — how likely it is to happen if we don't act

How likely is it to actually happen if we don't act?

Deadline — how close the mandatory date is

How soon is the date by which we must comply?

Are we paying for something a shared, company-wide system already does?

Is the spend hard to justify — no clear benefits, no owner, or it won't pay back in time?

5. Low strategic fit

Can we actually connect this to a stated company or business priority?

6. Incremental fragmentation

Is this yet another small one-off add-on, rather than part of a planned, bundled improvement?

Are we buying more licences or capacity while a lot of what we already own sits unused?

8. Deepens lock-in / raises exit cost

Does this make us more dependent on a supplier we plan to leave — harder or costlier to exit later?

9. Fully deferrable

Could we simply postpone this for a year or more with no real harm?

Named authority & instrument

Can we point to the actual law, regulation, or tax rule that requires this — chapter and verse?

Mandatory, not discretionary

Does the rule genuinely force this, or is it really our own choice or best practice?

Applicability confirmed (Legal / Compliance / Tax)

Has someone qualified (Legal / Compliance / Tax) confirmed the rule really applies to this specific part of Philips?

Independent second-line validation

Has an independent team — not the sponsor — formally signed this off?

Minimum-viable scope

Are we doing only what the rule requires, or adding 'nice-to-have' extras on top?

Impact — how serious the consequence is if we don't comply

If we don't comply, how serious is the consequence?

Likelihood — how likely it is to happen if we don't act

How likely is it to actually happen if we don't act?

Deadline — how close the mandatory date is

How soon is the date by which we must comply?

Establish a consolidated enterprise Master Data Management capability on IDMC for customer and vendor master data, improving data consistency, regulatory compliance, reporting accuracy and governance. The initiative will reduce duplicate master data management effort, improve operational efficiency, support Sunshine Act reporting requirements, and provide trusted enterprise master data for HCO/HCP, analytics, AI and business processes.
License Cost Reduction.

Without this investment Philips will continue to incur between €2.2M and €2.6M in operational and platform-related costs while maintaining fragmented customer and vendor master data solutions. Regulatory reporting obligations such as Sunshine Act requirements will remain difficult to manage, data governance risks will increase, duplicate data management effort will continue, and enterprise analytics, AI and business processes will be impacted by inconsistent master data.
Savings not realized

Customer, Vendor, Health Care Professional (HCP) and Health Care Organization (HCO) master data currently reside across multiple systems and data sources, resulting in fragmented business partner information, duplicate records, inconsistent governance and significant reconciliation effort. Sunshine Act reporting and HCO/HCP spend transparency require a single trusted source of governed master data, however the current landscape does not provide consolidated visibility across business partners. This creates compliance, reporting and operational risks, limits downstream application effectiveness, and increases the effort required to support regulatory reporting and enterprise business processes.

Consolidation of Business partners by moving customers master data and vendor master data as well to IDMC (MDM SaaS). Implement an enterprise Master Data Management capability on the IDMC platform by consolidating customer and vendor master data into a single governed master data service. The scope includes migration of master data domains, implementation of governance workflows, business partner harmonization, data quality controls, integration services, regulatory reporting support, deployment and establishment of a trusted enterprise master data foundation for all Business Partners including Health Care Professionals and Health Care Organizations.

This is not simply funding for future enhancements. It retains the only dedicated technical capability responsible for resolving complex intranet and SharePoint issues, managing global incidents, supporting GDPR and other legal or compliance-related changes, and maintaining a business-critical global employee platform.
 
The intranet protects at least €720,000 in annual employee-productivity value through faster access to information, tools and relevant content.
 
This is based on a deliberately conservative assumption:
60,000 employees save one minute per month
This equals 1,000 hours saved per month
At a fully loaded hourly cost of €60, this represents €60,000 per month
Annual value: €720,000
This calculation excludes further value created through self-service publishing, workflow automation, reduced operational support, personalized performance dashboards, enterprise communications, knowledge sharing and brand consistency.
 
The intranet is a key control for making required employee information available through a single, controlled and auditable global channel. This includes whistleblowing routes, AI and cybersecurity requirements, pay criteria, employment-related policies, and country-specific content required by local laws and regulations.
 
The dedicated development capacity is also needed to implement legal and regulatory changes in the platform. This includes creating or updating targeted pages and applying audience targeting so that content is available only to the relevant countries, employee groups or markets where required. For example, changes in local employment, diversity and inclusion, or other regulatory requirements may require rapid updates to content, access or visibility.
 
It also supports the management of SharePoint incidents, such as potential personal-data exposure, inappropriate access to content or other GDPR-related issues. Without this capability, Philips risks fragmented local communication, inconsistent implementation across countries and a reduced ability to demonstrate that required information was available to the right employees.
 
The intranet does not replace formal training, acknowledgement or case-management systems. It provides the trusted, governed employee-facing gateway that supports them.
 
The potential regulatory exposure is significant. Depending on applicability and national implementation, NIS2 can require maximum administrative fines of at least €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover for essential entities; whistleblowing obligations are enforced through national law; and EU pay-transparency rules can shift the burden of proof in equal-pay claims.
 
Without this dedicated capacity, Philips would face:
Longer resolution times for complex intranet and SharePoint defects, resulting in degraded user experience and disruption for employees.
No established specialist owner for global SharePoint incidents, increasing response times and business impact.
Delayed or stopped improvements to employee experience, automation, accessibility, performance and dashboards, while the backlog continues to grow.
Delayed content-lifecycle and governance work, increasing compliance risk and future remediation effort.
Delayed implementation of regulatory or legal changes, including required country-specific pages and targeted content.
A weaker intranet as the central gateway to the digital employee experience, resulting in fragmented journeys, continued manual work and reduced trust in the platform.
Less reliable access to relevant business information and personalized performance data, weakening strategic alignment.
Loss of accumulated platform knowledge, requiring supplier re-onboarding, discovery and knowledge transfer before delivery could restart in the future.
 
The decision is not between spending and saving €175,000. It is between retaining the dedicated technical capability for Philips’ global employee platform and accepting at least €720,000 in annual productivity value at risk, together with slower incident resolution, growing operational and compliance risk, and loss of a trusted digital gateway for employees.
 
Beyond the quantified value, the investment enables more consistent enterprise communications, faster business-change implementation, stronger knowledge sharing, personalized performance dashboards, and a coherent Philips employee experience across connected digital touchpoints.

The global SharePoint intranet is the centre of Philips’ digital employee experience and the central gateway through which approximately 70,000 employees access trusted information, business updates, digital tools, enterprise communications and personalized performance dashboards.
The intranet is not a static communications site. While standard SharePoint capabilities support basic publishing, Philips requires dedicated technical expertise to deliver and maintain tailored functionality, integrations, automation, performance improvements, accessibility, governance and content lifecycle management. Content lifecycle management is also required to support Philips’ legal and compliance obligations across the SharePoint environment.
The external Intranet Development Team is Philips’ only dedicated specialist capability currently assigned to resolve complex technical intranet issues, maintain and improve the global platform, and support SharePoint incidents and technical issues at global scale in close collaboration with Philips IT. The team also enables high-impact capabilities such as personalized performance dashboards, giving employees direct access to business-relevant metrics based on their organizational profile.
Continued funding is required both to retain essential technical ownership and incident-response capability and to deliver the roadmap of employee-experience, automation, governance and performance improvements. Without it, there is no alternative dedicated capability to diagnose, fix and prevent technical intranet issues, while the backlog of planned improvements will grow.

This investment retains the dedicated team that keeps Philips’ global employee intranet reliable, secure and continuously improving. The team provides the specialized SharePoint development capability needed to resolve complex technical issues, support global incidents and deliver strategic platform enhancements that cannot be achieved through standard SharePoint configuration alone.

•	Resolution of complex technical intranet issues and support for SharePoint incidents and platform-wide issues at global scale, in close collaboration with Philips IT.
•	Development and maintenance of tailored intranet functionality, reusable components, integrations, automation and workflows.
•	Continuous improvements to user experience, performance, navigation, search, mobile usability and accessibility.
•	Ongoing support and enhancement of personalized, data-rich performance dashboards embedded on the intranet homepage.
•	Implementation and maintenance of governance, content lifecycle-management and compliance-related solutions across the SharePoint environment.
•	Delivery of standardized global SharePoint solutions and support for consistent digital branding across relevant Microsoft collaboration tools.
•	Support for strategic enterprise initiatives that require SharePoint-development expertise.
The team supports both day-to-day technical stability and the prioritized roadmap of improvements that keep the intranet secure, scalable, user-friendly and aligned with Philips’ evolving business and employee needs.

Financial value at risk – what this investment protects:
– Share price: Philips is worth about €21.4B (25 Sep 2026). Each 1% share-price fall wipes out about €214M. Across 125 reputation crises, listed companies lost on average 5% of value in the first year (about €1.1B for Philips) and badly handled cases up to 30% (Pentland Analytics/Aon, 2018).
– Precedents of results published too early: ASML fell 16% (more than $52B) on the day its results appeared early on its own website (Oct 2024); Google fell 9% before trading was halted (2012); Twitter fell about 18% before trading was halted (2015). In each case the error made the fall happen uncontrolled, during trading, before management could explain – and made headlines.
– Fines: Maximum fines: EU MAR 2% of turnover or more (about €360M), EU AI Act up to 3% (about €540M), GDPR up to 4% (about €720M).
– Brand value: Interbrand values the Philips brand at $10.6B (about €9.1B, 2025); each 1% is about €91M.
Break-even: the €1.0M requested (EW-175 + EW-176) equals 0.005% of Philips' market value – about 0.1 euro cent per share. A 1% trust discount would cost 214 times the investment.
Finish what we started: completes the business case of the about €1.9M invested in 2025–2026 (2025 case €630K, AOP 2026 €1.05M, about €0.2M added by IT). That case counted on lower AEM licence and maintenance costs; the MVP delivered the switch-off, not yet the full benefit.

Financial impact if it goes wrong:
– Investor trust: a premature, late or leaked results release can trigger a trading halt and a share-price fall – each 1% is about €214M of shareholder value; reputation crises cost listed companies 5% of value on average in the first year (about €1.1B for Philips).
– Regulator: AFM investigation and fines (precedent: €2M for SBM Offshore), legal maximums of 2–4% of turnover (€360–720M), and possible investor claims (Philips is also listed on the NYSE).
– Brand: each 1% of brand value lost is about €91M.
What goes wrong without the investment:
1. Results, M&A and other timed announcements go out too early (embargoed files reachable via a direct PAL link) or too late (PAL uploads take up to 30 minutes and there is no direct upload in Contentful as back-up). From the Q4 2026 results this applies to the regulated results release itself.
2. Content can go live on a single click without approval – unintended or premature publications that damage Philips' reputation or release market-sensitive information early, now across more self-publishing country teams. When results move to philips.com, the four-eyes control of today's results process would be lost.
3. Locale legal requirements to be solved: Italy cannot apply its legally required notice and wording page by page; Russia keeps governance information hidden; Canada's required pages have no home unless moved before the switch-off.
4. Local terms of use stay outdated and AI-generated content is not labelled – exposure under the EU AI Act.
6. The replatforming stays a minimum version and will not deliver its business case: deferred features never arrive, release defects continue, and there is no aftercare after the global and US go-live – the €1.9M investment delivers the switch-off but not its business case.
Without 2027 funding, even small legally required changes cannot be released: each needs development and quality validation, and the old platform is gone as a fallback.

Summary: philips.com is where Philips meets its legal publication duties for the whole company (Corporate, HS, PH): market-sensitive announcements, investor and governance information, the Philips-wide privacy notice and legal notices in 90+ locales. The 2025–2026 replatforming (about €1.9M) went live as a minimum viable product (MVP) to switch off the old platform (AEM) on time: pages and templates work, but legal controls and features the business case relied on were deferred because of budget and timeline. Each legal gap below was raised by Legal, Privacy Legal, External Relations or a country team.

A. Legal and regulatory gaps
1. Timed, market-sensitive releases depend on PAL (Philips' image and document library). Quarterly and annual results press releases and other time-critical announcements (e.g. acquisitions, divestments, bonds) are timed to the minute; External Relations: some releases must be online within 25–30 minutes to meet regulatory obligations. Yet every file (e.g. the press release PDF) must go through PAL: an upload can take up to 30 minutes, and a replaced file can take hours to show on the live site. There is no back-up: files cannot be uploaded directly in Contentful, which is a hard requirement for regulated releases. Embargoed files are exposed too: a draft PDF or image can be opened via a direct PAL link before release (requirements for a restricted PAL area went to IT on 22 Sep 2026; IT is now scoping it – no solution or estimate yet). Result: files go live too early or too late. From the Q4 2026 results, results publication moves from the Results Hub to philips.com (see EW-176), so this hits the regulated release itself. What is at stake showed on 27 July 2026, when the Q2 results went live early via the Results Hub: a 30-minute trading halt and formal AFM and SEC filings.
2. No approval workflow: the MVP delivered templates and components, but no approval workflows are built in yet. Content goes live without a second approval, while country teams now publish themselves (self-service). External Relations requires approval workflows (8 Sep 2026). This governance is critical: without it, content can go live unintended or too early – damaging Philips' reputation, or releasing market-sensitive information before its time. 
3. Privacy notice pages: Privacy Legal requires each privacy notice as one page on the global domain with all languages and a language selector. The new platform has no such set-up – it builds one page per locale. The page also does not show the visitor's country, so the required country-specific privacy information (e.g. US, Japan, Taiwan, Turkey, China, Brazil, EEA) is missing. Privacy Legal: "This is a requirement." Some locales have no working terms of use (e.g. Slovenia, Belarus).
4. Country rules the templates cannot meet. Italy: a legally required notice (medical-device content is for journalists and healthcare professionals only) can only be switched on or off for a whole section, and required wording (Legislative Decree 231/2001) does not fit the component. Russia: words break mid-word (also in English), so Executive Committee and Supervisory Board information is hidden. Canada: the required accessibility (AODA) and forced-labour pages are still on the old platform.
5. EU AI Act (transparency rules from 2 August 2026): Legal's AI-Act changes to the terms of use must reach all 90+ local sites, and AI-generated images and content need visible, screen-reader and machine-readable labels. More work is expected once Legal finalises its guidance.

B. Finish what we started
The MVP delivered the switch-off, not yet the value. Features were deferred (e.g. advanced media library, experience improvements, GEO / AI findability  enhancements), testing coverage is limited (2026 releases caused download and language defects) and there is no funded aftercare (no January release planned). Without completion, the replatforming does not deliver its business case.

2027 scope – A. legal controls (Priority 1) and B. completion of the replatforming (carry-over):
A1. Controlled release of market-sensitive content: (a) direct asset upload in Contentful (PDFs, images) as fast lane and back-up to PAL for quarterly and annual results press releases and other time-critical announcements, so every file is live at the minute of release; (b) embargo protection in PAL: a restricted group, protection of the file address itself (including thumbnails and renditions), automatic release linked to the publishing workflow, restrictions re-applied if publication is postponed, per-user access logs; (c) publishing to the minute, editing lock during results, confirmation that publication succeeded, audit trail.
A2. Approval workflows and publishing rights (governance): approval workflows built into Contentful – a recorded second approval before anything goes live (four-eyes principle); a stricter flow with sign-off by the content owner (e.g. External Relations, Investor Relations, Legal) for market-sensitive and legal pages; publishing and scheduling only after approval; role-based publishing rights for country publishers; an audit trail of who approved what and when (also evidence of human review for AI-assisted content under the AI Act); and flagging of rights-restricted, single-use images in PAL (e.g. a partner CEO photo) to prevent unlicensed reuse.
A3. Privacy and legal notice set-up: each privacy notice (Philips-wide and app notices) as one page on the global domain with all languages and a language selector, showing the country section that applies to the visitor; complete terms of use and cookie notices for every locale; removal of outdated notices; stable addresses for legally referenced documents; complete 5-year archive of regulated announcements.
A4. Country legal requirements: legal notices and pop-ups set per page and per country (Italy first); components that can hold mandatory legal wording; correct line breaks in all languages (Russia first); Canada AODA and forced-labour pages.
A5. EU AI Act: roll-out of AI-Act terms-of-use and house-rule changes to all 90+ locales; AI-content labels (visible, alt text, machine-readable); disclosure for any AI assistant on the site (e.g. planned supplier chatbot); follow-up of Legal's guidance.
A6. Compliance assurance: every change validated under the website's quality process (releases are QMS-assessed) with Legal sign-off.
B. Finish what we started: the features deferred from the MVP (advanced media library, experience improvements, GEO / AI findability enhancements), automated regression testing to stop release defects, and aftercare after the global and US go-live.

Results hub replatforming (Quarterly and annual financial reporting)

The reason for this investment: on 27 July 2026 the external platform released the Q2 2026 results early, during US trading hours. This forced an unplanned market disclosure by the Board of Management and Disclosure Committee, formal AFM and SEC (6-K) filings and a 30-minute trading halt. This investment removes the cause: results are released only by Philips, on the Philips platform, through a controlled manual step.
Financial value at risk:
– Share price: each 1% fall is about €214M of shareholder value (Philips market value about €21.4B, 25 Sep 2026). Precedent: ASML fell 16% (more than $52B) on the day its results appeared early on its own website (Oct 2024).
– Fines: the AFM fined SBM Offshore €2M for late disclosure of inside information (2019); the EU MAR maximum is 2% of turnover or more (about €360M).
Break-even: the €400K requested equals about 0.002% of Philips' market value – under 0.2% of what a 1% share-price fall would cost.

Hard benefit: €178K per year once the external Results Hub platform is retired (€118K platform and licence fees, about €60K operational and maintenance support); payback about 2.2 years.
Other benefits (Disclosure Committee paper): one simple corporate publication channel, direct Philips ownership and control, fewer parties with clearer ownership, results aligned with the Investor Relations and Communications pages.

This has already gone wrong: on 27 July 2026 the Q2 2026 results went live early from the external platform, during US trading hours – with a 30-minute trading halt and formal AFM and SEC (6-K) filings as a result.
Without the investment:
1. The Disclosure Committee-aligned move of results publication to philips.com cannot be executed. Results stay on a vendor platform where one vendor script error released market-sensitive information early.
2. The Q3 2026 set-up is a temporary workaround: manual publication, extra reviews by Group Accounting & Reporting and Philips IT, and uploads in the early morning of results day, outside NL and US trading hours. It depends on people and vendor commitments, not on controls Philips owns.
3. A repeat after a known incident would be hard to defend to investors and the AFM: another trading halt, an unplanned market disclosure, AFM scrutiny and fines of up to 2% of turnover under EU MAR (about €360M), and a share-price impact of about €214M per 1%.
4. Complex governance across multiple parties and vendor dependency continue (Disclosure Committee paper).
5. €178K per year of avoidable external platform and support costs continues.

What happened: on 27 July 2026 at 7.30pm CET the Q2 2026 results press release went live ahead of schedule (planned: 28 July, 7am CET), during US trading hours. Cause: a software (script) error in the external vendor's set-up of the Results Hub publishing platform – it published the results immediately on upload instead of at the scheduled time. The Board of Management and Disclosure Committee had to convene immediately and publish the Q2 results promptly, in line with market rules. Formal AFM and SEC (6-K) filings followed on 28 July, and trading was halted for 30 minutes.
Control gap: Philips' most market-sensitive publication runs on a vendor-hosted platform outside the Philips IT landscape. Philips cannot itself control, test or sign off the software that releases its results, and ownership is spread over several parties (Group Accounting & Reporting, Communications, Investor Relations and the vendor).
Decision: the intended approach, aligned with the Disclosure Committee, is to decommission the Results Hub, publish results on philips.com (Contentful, the Philips platform) and run the publication in-house with Philips IT. The Disclosure Committee paper to the Board of Management (28 Sep 2026) states that this requires IT investment and prioritisation, starting in Q4 2026, to be ready by year-end.
Interim only: the Q3 2026 results (3 November) stay on the vendor platform as the only viable option, protected by manual workarounds – manual publication, extra reviews by Group Accounting & Reporting and Philips IT, and uploads outside NL and US trading hours.

Scope (intended approach, aligned with the Disclosure Committee):
1. Publication channel: quarterly and annual results (press release, results presentation, financial and ESG content) published on philips.com; the external Results Hub website is decommissioned.
2. Platform: results pages, documents and data feeds move to Contentful (Philips platform) within the Philips IT landscape, integrated with the Investor Relations and corporate pages.
3. In-house operation: publication executed by Philips, with clear end-to-end ownership – Group Accounting & Reporting (functional) and Philips IT (technical) – and a results-day support runbook.
4. Release controls: publication only through a deliberate, approved manual step (no automatic publication); four-eyes approval with evidence; protected preview and embargoed files; publishing to the minute; rollback; documented testing and formal Philips sign-off before any change goes live.
5. Resilience of the single channel: cache and peak-load management, certificate ownership, monitoring and fallback, because philips.com becomes the only results channel.
Timing: initial build in Q4 2026 for readiness by year-end; 2027 completes the migration, runs the first full results year in-house and decommissions the Results Hub.
Out of scope: replacement of Workiva, SAP BW, the CAT editor, regulated financial source data, report generation, ESEF/SEC iXBRL filing and statutory PDF production – these stay the controlled systems of record and do need to be integrated.

Internal Controls Automation will strengthen Philips’ control environment by moving from largely manual control monitoring and testing activities to automated, continuous assurance capabilities. The initiative will provide real-time visibility into IT application controls through dashboards, enabling earlier detection of compliance issues, faster remediation, and improved governance across Finance and IT processes.
Key qualitative benefits include:
•	Enhanced Compliance & Risk Management
Improved Audit Readiness
Stronger Internal Control Environment
Increased Operational Efficiency
Faster Issue Detection and Resolution
Data-Driven Decision Making
Foundation for AI-Driven Controls Monitoring
Sustainable Operating Model

• IT application-control monitoring and testing will remain largely manual and periodic, limiting continuous assurance across Finance and IT processes.
• Control failures and compliance exceptions may be detected late, increasing the likelihood of audit findings, financial-reporting risk and remediation costs.
• Finance, Controls and IT teams will continue spending significant effort collecting evidence, testing controls and preparing audit responses.
• Limited real-time dashboards and consolidated insights will reduce management visibility, slow issue escalation and weaken accountability for remediation.
• The ADL-based monitoring capability, Zone 3 operational handover and Zone 2 AI scoping agent will be delayed, increasing dependency on fragmented manual solutions.
• Planned AI-enabled productivity gains, cost savings and progress toward a scalable continuous-controls operating model will not be realized.
Current capabilities do not adequately support implementation of automation IT application controls continuous monitoring/testing. This prevents planned productivity and cost savings.
